title: 🍄 Peoples of the Second Age II — Ents, Centaurs, Merfolk & Other Traditions
rawNotionMarkup: Second Age people-by-people annals, Part II: twelve widely varied peoples. These are specific ancient local incidents and cultural developments, newly authorized and revisable. The names Awakening (Years 1–321), Wonder (322–1,321) and Fire (1,322–1,437) are Avarran chronological terms used for cross-continental dating; no other continent is presumed to share them. There are no Orcs in this Age. ## Ents — a patient being can still be wrong Years 1–321: Some Ent stewards protected woodland ecosystems through the independent World's Breath while older lunar cycles were disturbed. The Trial of the Fallen Hollow concerned a great fallen tree blocking a poor farming community's only safe road. One Ent assembly demanded it remain untouched for forest renewal; another argued that living roots must not demand human deaths. After several travelers froze, Willow-Walks-Slowly, an Ent witness, apologized publicly and helped negotiate a path that preserved the hollow as a nursery while maintaining a road. Other groves refused to copy the arrangement. Years 322–1,321: In selected woodland councils, Ents taught woodland recovery and co-developed living flood buffers with Eldar, Mushroom folk and local farmers, while disagreeing about commercial clearing. The Rings of the Patient Grove recorded disputed stewardship promises by living marks and later paper copies; no Ent conveyed an authentic written pre-Cataclysm history. A few Ent communities withdrew from all negotiating, while others came to respect shorter-lived neighbors who would not live to see the results of certain decisions. Years 1,322–1,437: Vaelora's later grove disputes and woodland compacts reflect compatible tensions without imposing one Ent government or species-wide position. ## Centaurs — no single road is the right way Years 1–321: Centaur families in open grasslands, river markets and dry savannas charted safe water and seasonal routes when lunar wayfinding failed. the Three-Spring Dispute involved a coalition of mobile Centaur households and several villages whose governors declared a common watering place private property. Violence followed, with damaged fields and injured travelers. Asha Reed-Stirrup, a Centaur mother, negotiated marked access corridors and compensation for damaged crops. She faced criticism from her own kin for conceding anything to settled landlords. Years 322–1,321: Some Centaur academies developed astronomy, healing, weather observation and sophisticated contract law, while others resisted the fee-controlled monopoly of city schools. the Charter of Open Paths was accepted in several Sahradi and Orundel settlements to recognize customary passage without surrendering local public safety powers. Wealthy horse-and-cart guilds tried to exploit its wording to claim land, so traveling families demanded strict definitions. Centaur lives included city families, craftspeople, scholars and independent farmers; an assumed nomadic destiny is noncanon. Years 1,322–1,437: The Era of Fire includes local pastoral disputes, not a single Centaur empire or established Orc alliance. ## Merfolk — sovereignty beneath the surface Years 1–321: Independent saltwater and inland-water Merfolk polities recalibrated depth soundings and current observation after magical navigation became unpredictable. In the Sunken Sounding, a reef community found that surface sailors had been following an enchanted signal into dangerous rocks. A Merfolk pilot, Kelara Deep-Current, led rescue efforts even as an offshore lord threatened her people for crossing his claimed waters. Her polity answered that the sea was not the lord's estate. A later local agreement recognized a route of emergency access but left fisheries disputes unresolved. Years 322–1,321: Tide academies, current-craft, underwater healing and art grew with new lunar disciplines. The Blue Shell Negotiations between one Merfolk city and a shore port challenged demands that underwater laborers work off debts imposed by surface merchants. Several captives were released; some debts were merely transferred. The event was remembered in Merfolk songs as the beginning, not the victory, of a longer campaign for fair trade. No universal underwater monarchy or invented shared moon-deity results. Years 1,322–1,437: Some northern and Orundel warning compacts involved Merfolk observers; each underwater state remained politically independent. ## Giants — a large hand can build or crush Years 1–321: Giant settlements in uplands and coldlands rebuilt shelters with direct stonework when some moon-powered wards failed. At the Split-Snow Causeway, a Giant quarry patron charged small villages ruinous rates for essential winter stone. A younger Giant mason, Bramm Long-Hearth, offered repairs at ordinary labor costs and was expelled from his patron's household. His new workshop welcomed apprentices of several peoples. Other Giant clans distrusted all valley settlements; no shared moral character is fixed. Years 322–1,321: Regional Giant masons and sky observers enriched high-altitude roads, bridges and public festivals, while some nobles used new magical lifting works to seize quarries and debt labor. the Hill-Gate Petition challenged compulsory work on a monumental arch. A negotiated settlement paid some workers and protected a local shelter from demolition; it did not end all coercive labor. Stories of Giant courtiers, poets and stern family elders coexisted with those of isolated highland herdspeople. Years 1,322–1,437: The later Rock-and-Star traditions and Tharvorn local rescue history do not resolve the existence or origin of Living Mountains. ## Kobolds — every tunnel is also somebody's home Years 1–321: Kobold neighborhoods learned to test ventilation, excavate escape routes and maintain unenchanted lighting as magical supports became uncertain. In the Ash-Pipe Collapse, a profitable mine ignored the warnings of Vekri Six-Marks, an independent Kobold inspector. Several workers died. Families won the right to post dangerous-section marks without the mine owner's approval, although they were not all compensated. Some Kobold communities rejected mining altogether, living as farmers, librarians and urban craftworkers. Years 322–1,321: New compact light magic, ventilation and ore tests enriched some Kobold guilds. the Lantern Exchange was an association of independent small workshops that rented devices to poor settlements at reasonable cost while resisting an aristocratic monopoly. Its founders quarreled over profit shares, and one workshop withheld designs during a shortage. Members eventually adopted a rule allowing essential emergency ventilation designs to be freely copied. This was an act of local institutional choice, not a biological instinct for engineering. Years 1,322–1,437: Kobold work in mixed cities and new regional states need not imply they became the servants of any single dominant people. ## Satyrs and Fauns — celebration is not consent Years 1–321: Some orchard and meadow societies held ordinary feasts and songs when dangerous magical festivities were abandoned. the Last Orchard Song commemorated a settlement that chose to share seed grain rather than burn it for an elaborate rite. Its chief celebrant, Miri Bell-Hoof, was condemned by a neighboring priestly patron for disrespecting tradition. The orchard survived a lean season, but several households later returned to the patron's more ostentatious celebrations. The story is about difficult choices, not one universal Satyr temperament. Years 322–1,321: Diverse Satyr and Faun artists, healers, farmers and scholars adopted newly mastered lunar arts. the Festival of Borrowed Bread in a particular Vaeloran woodland market used public performance to raise aid for indebted families. Wealthy sponsors tried to forbid songs criticizing estate collectors; musicians performed them anyway and some were arrested. A later civic hearing allowed criticism at civic festivals, but not all courts respected the judgment. A quiet Satyr farmer uninterested in song remained as ordinary a citizen as a famous performer. Years 1,322–1,437: The later Vaeloran orchard controversies did not make every festive group part of one political league. ## Pixies — small does not mean powerless Years 1–321: Pixie communities exposed to dangerous changing lunar flight and shelter wards built physical windbreaks, repairable roofs and warning signs. The Feather-Glass Storm destroyed a small cliff-side neighborhood; larger nearby residents refused to spend labor replacing tiny dwellings. Ressa Flintwing, a Pixie elected steward, coordinated mutual repair and compelled a market court to treat destroyed miniature housing as genuine property rather than decoration. Her petition succeeded in one district; others mocked it. Years 322–1,321: Pixie messenger networks and intricate lunar craft flourished where safe practice and independent education were available. the Lantern-Ladder Strike protested wealthy patrons assigning dangerous high-ward maintenance to poorly paid Pixie apprentices. Several older Pixie guilds had participated in the exploitation. Their eventual reforms distinguished skilled work from disposable labor and required a named adult supervisor. Pixie towns retained governments, kin disputes, theaters and serious politics, hidden or public. Years 1,322–1,437: The later Lantern Orchard and forest arts do not make all Pixie settlements Aelwyn Fae courts. ## Minotaurs — law does not come from the shape of a maze Years 1–321: Independent Minotaur households and civic networks across savannas, river cities and uplands maintained ordinary evacuation and building plans when enchantments failed. the Twelve Door Petition accused a city governor of building a confusing ceremonial hall without safe public exits. Jemek of the Straight Path, a Minotaur legal advocate, persuaded the court that a grand work's beauty could not excuse trapping citizens inside it. The resulting safety rule applied to public buildings, not to a worldwide labyrinth religion. Years 322–1,321: Some Minotaur schools became known for architecture, spatial enchantments, navigation and philosophy; elsewhere independent farmers, administrators, artists and soldiers followed different traditions. the Wide Hall Confrontation arose when a ruling family tried to convert free apprentices into hereditary guard retainers. A coalition of guardians, teachers and apprentices achieved a charter limiting compulsory service. A few noble houses continued to flout it. No Minotaur-wide monarchy, uniform honor code or magical instinct was imposed. Years 1,322–1,437: Sahradi local councils and legal debates could contain Minotaur representatives without subordinating the species to the Blue-Jar Crown. ## Brownies and Boggarts — paid work, chosen work Years 1–321: Small household and neighborhood communities performed vital maintenance when domestic lunar wards failed. the Chimney Counting began as a petition to record the workers who had repaired a dangerous winter heating network. A town's rulers initially credited a grand enchanted household instead; Palla Hearth-Thread, a Brownie public advocate, presented repair marks and witnesses that forced recognition of the working families. In some towns the result was wages; elsewhere it only brought grudging acknowledgment. Brownies and Boggarts were never defined as compulsory invisible servants. Years 322–1,321: Their independent craft guilds, living quarters, warning systems and magical practices flourished alongside exploitation by wealthy households. the Doorway Covenant in several small settlements prohibited a homeowner from claiming ownership of the people who lived or worked within the home, while allowing negotiated paid services. Some Boggart groups preferred hidden lives; others established visible neighborhood councils. Their relationship as biological lineages or cultural labels remains undetermined. Years 1,322–1,437: Later Vaeloran household labor and orchard relations reflect local patterns, not a universal Brownie–Boggart identity. ## Trolls — tolls, homes and divided rivers Years 1–321: Distinct Troll riverside and upland communities made physical crossings dependable during erratic magic. The Stonepot Ford became known for a Troll widow, Hura Greybank, who imposed a posted fixed toll rather than the arbitrary payments demanded by her predecessor. Travelers still complained that the crossing was costly; her neighbors argued the money funded winter repairs. Farther downstream, a predatory band robbed crossings, and local Troll settlements resisted being blamed for the raids. Years 322–1,321: New river-sensing and bridge magic helped some Troll engineers and judges; other households farmed, taught children or avoided trade routes altogether. In the Quay-Water Judgment, a Troll magistrate ordered an independent port to restore a floodplain it had ruined while extracting gravel. Enforcers were bribed and delayed repairs, so local families themselves built temporary defenses while appealing the ruling. The outcome was a partial settlement, not universal fairness. Years 1,322–1,437: The later working communities and the Frost-Hearth Confederation do not establish universal Troll regeneration, sunlight weakness, or one king for all Trolls. ## Mushroom folk — the knowledge hidden in rot Years 1–321: Mushroom folk families and scientific circles studied decay, moisture and food safety as lunar influences changed; they could rely on the independent World's Breath without all becoming one networked mind. the Bitter Cellar was an investigation into poisoned winter stores in a mixed settlement. Viri Soft-Gill, a Mushroom folk researcher, proved the problem came from neglected airflow rather than an invented curse. The local lord withheld her report because its publication would expose his warehouse contractor. Workers leaked copies, and neighboring towns improved sanitation. Years 322–1,321: New moon-derived cultivation and healing techniques enriched fungi farms, dye works and medicine. the Spore-Quota Dispute concerned a tax on medicinal products that priced ordinary sick households out of care. Several growers developed an independent distribution network; guild authorities accused them of stealing trade secrets. A compromise limited exclusive licenses on essential treatments in one city. Their exact biology, lifespans and reproductive mechanisms remain unassigned, with no hive-mind mandate. Years 1,322–1,437: Mushrooms, soil and medicine continued to matter amid later political conflicts, without linking these communities to the dark mages. ## Harpies — a warning given freely Years 1–321: Harpy cliff and coast settlements used physical signals and landmark charts when moon-touched flight and weather rites became uncertain. the Broken Cry remembers a cliff harbor whose ruling patrol ordered warnings withheld from an enemy ship during a storm. Several Harpy guides defied the order to save the crew; two were later imprisoned for aiding outsiders. Their community divided sharply about military duty and rescue ethics. Years 322–1,321: Distinct aerial town councils developed warning systems, cliff architecture, performances and lunar navigation techniques. the Sky-Message Charter in a few Orundel and northern ports required public warning of deadly storms regardless of a vessel's allegiance. A faction argued that this endangered defenders during war; supporters argued that no banner could change the sea's danger. The law was imperfect and geographically limited, and Harpy livelihoods extended far beyond messenger work. Years 1,322–1,437: Later river-bell and cliff warning practices could draw on this history without forming a single worldwide Harpy institution. ## Limits of the account No Orcs, Urakai cities, or Orc-linked alliances are present in the Second Age. No truly original First Age records survive; all reliable documents begin later. No species is inherently vicious, cowardly, servile or virtuous. Magical techniques do not restore powers permanently lost with shattered moon sources. The ancient polities described do not pre-establish current states, modern census values or Gloin Hammerfeld's genealogy.
